recs.x: Plans should cover biological, chemical, environmental, unknown and other relevant threats.
Regular risk profiling should be built into planning.
The One Health approach should be strengthened, with cross-sector collaboration across human, animal and environmental health.
Recovery should be treated as an essential part of incident response and reflected in plans.
Crisis-relevant medical countermeasures should be part of plans (stockpiling, manufacturing, supply chains, innovation) with a clear account of how they complement each other.
Plans should set out emergency research and innovation strategies, including fast ways to assess and approve research and mobilise dedicated funding.
Plans should describe coordination with EU institutions and cross-border and EU-level support mechanisms.
Regular testing, including simulation exercises and in-action and after-action reviews, should inform plan updates.
Laboratory systems should scale up rapidly in emergencies: forecast surge testing needs, establish scale-up strategies (including the commercial sector) and test them regularly.
Surveillance should be digital and interoperable, linking laboratory, clinical and epidemiological data across sectors for early warning and all-hazards monitoring.
The One Health approach should be fully implemented, with stronger coordination, surveillance and information sharing, and attention to climate effects on zoonotic risks.
AMR National Action Plans should be current, funded and aligned with EU targets, backed by IPC and antimicrobial stewardship in all healthcare settings.

eu.area: Response, surge capacity and continuity of essential services

recs.x: Health workforce surge plans should be reviewed and tested regularly; long-term workforce needs assessed; procedures set up to mobilise extra personnel, including cross-border deployments.

Crisis-relevant MCMs should be held in risk-based strategic stockpiles, managed sustainably (rotation, expiry management, virtual stocks) and supported by legal frameworks; supply monitored, demand assessed and production scaled up.
Public health and social measures should follow a clear evidence-based framework with real-time evaluation.
Essential health services should continue under tested business continuity plans; border regions should have procedures for cross-border patient transfers when clinically required.
Risk communication plans should be ready to activate, regularly evaluated and support inclusive community engagement.
